title: Nixon's Handshake With Zhou Enlai
text:
On February 21, 1972, Air Force One landed in Beijing. It was the first visit by an American president to the People's Republic of China, after more than twenty years in which the two countries had no diplomatic relations and treated each other as enemies.

In his memoirs Richard Nixon explains how carefully he planned the first moment. He knew that Premier Zhou Enlai had felt insulted at the Geneva Conference in 1954, when, according to the story widely believed in China, the American Secretary of State John Foster Dulles refused to shake his hand. Nixon was determined that this time the handshake would be unmistakable. He came down the steps of the plane with only his wife, while aides were told to stay aboard, and he held out his hand to Zhou as he reached the bottom.

The photograph went around the world. Nixon recalls that Zhou later told him, during the ride into the city, that his handshake had come over the vastest ocean in the world, twenty five years of no communication. The visit ended with the Shanghai Communique, which opened the way to normal relations between the two countries in 1979.
lesson: If you know someone carries the memory of a past slight, a deliberate gesture of respect can help undo it. Small symbols can matter a great deal in relationships.
source: Richard Nixon, RN: The Memoirs of Richard Nixon (1978)
caveat: Whether Dulles actually snubbed Zhou at Geneva in 1954 is disputed, though the story was widely believed and shaped the 1972 planning.
